answer: A traditional Finnish or Estonian sauna is usually heated to 70–90 °C at bench level. Beginners feel most comfortable around 60–70 °C. Remember that the upper bench is noticeably hotter than the lower one, so you can control the heat simply by changing where you sit.

Löyly – called leil in Estonian – is the burst of steam you get by ladling water onto the hot stones. Start with half a ladle, wait for the wave of heat to reach you, then add more if everyone agrees. Always ask the others before throwing – it is good sauna manners.

keywords: first;beginner;never been;first time;what to do;newbie;new to sauna;how to use a sauna
answer: For your first visit: shower first, take a towel to sit on, and start on the lower bench. Stay 5–10 minutes, then cool down outside or in a cool shower, rest and drink water. Two or three rounds is plenty. Listen to your body and leave whenever you feel uncomfortable.

topic: How long and how many rounds
keywords: how long;minutes;rounds;how many rounds;duration;stay in;how many times;session length
answer: A typical round in the hot room lasts 8–15 minutes, followed by a cool-down and a rest about as long as the heating round. Most people do 2–4 rounds. There is no need to compete – shorter rounds are perfectly fine.
You lose a lot of fluid through sweat, often 0.5–1 litre per session. Drink a glass of water before you start and between rounds. Water, herbal tea or a mild mineral drink are good choices.

Avoid alcohol before and during sauna. Alcohol together with heat lowers blood pressure, dehydrates you and increases the risk of fainting, falls and heart rhythm problems. Enjoy a cold drink of water instead – and save the beer for much later, if at all.

Cooling down is half of the sauna ritual. Options: a cool shower, a swim in a lake or the sea, rolling in snow or an ice hole (avanto). If you are new to cold plunges, start gently with a cool shower and keep cold dips short. People with heart conditions should ask a doctor before cold plunges.

A vihta (Estonian: viht) is a bundle of fresh birch branches. Gently patting the skin with a warmed whisk improves circulation and releases a fresh birch scent. Soak it in warm water for a few minutes before use; dried whisks need a longer soak in hot water.

keywords: store;storing;storage;freeze;frozen;dried;birch whisk;make a whisk;make my own;make whisks;make a birch whisk;make birch whisks;own whisk
answer: Fresh whisks are made in early summer when birch leaves are soft and strong. To store them, either dry them in a cool, airy and shady place, or wrap them in a bag and freeze them. A frozen whisk is thawed in warm water and feels almost like a fresh one.

A smoke sauna has no chimney: the stove heats a large pile of stones for several hours while the smoke fills the room, then the smoke is let out before bathing. The heat is soft and long-lasting. The Võro smoke sauna tradition in South Estonia is on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The main sauna heaters are wood-burning stoves (classic feel, softer steam, need a chimney), electric heaters (easy and clean, controlled by a thermostat) and continuous-heat vs. heat-storing models. For a home sauna, pick the heater power according to the room volume – roughly 1 kW per 1–1.5 m³ for a well-insulated room.

Use rocks made for sauna heaters, such as peridotite, olivine diabase or vulcanite. Check the stones once a year and replace cracked or crumbling ones – broken stones block air flow and can damage an electric heater. Rinse new stones before stacking them loosely, with air gaps between them.

Benches are usually made from aspen, alder or heat-treated wood because they stay cooler to the touch and have few knots or resin. Walls are often spruce or pine panelling. Avoid varnish on benches – use only sauna oil or wax made for sauna surfaces.

Good ventilation keeps the air fresh and the löyly pleasant. A common setup has a fresh-air inlet low near the heater and an exhaust vent high on the opposite wall or low under the bench. Ventilate and dry the sauna after every use to prevent mould.

keywords: clean;cleaning;wash;mould;mold;maintenance;care;dirty;stain;clean the benches;clean benches;clean the sauna;clean my sauna
answer: After each use leave the door and vents open so the room dries. Every few weeks wash benches with mild soap or a special sauna cleaner and a soft brush. Always sit on a towel – it keeps the benches clean. Sand off dark stains lightly once a year.

topic: How long does it take to heat
keywords: heat up;heating up;preheat;warm up;how long to heat;ready;how long does it take;stay warm;stays warm
answer: An electric sauna usually heats up in 30–60 minutes. A wood-burning sauna takes about 45–90 minutes, depending on the stove, the wood and the outdoor temperature. A smoke sauna needs 4–6 hours of heating.

Shower before entering, sit on a towel, ask before throwing more löyly and keep your voice low. In Finnish and Estonian public saunas men and women usually have separate rooms and people bathe nude; in mixed saunas swimsuits or towels are common. Follow the local rules.

Regular sauna bathing helps many people relax, sleep better and recover after exercise. Some long-term studies link frequent sauna use to better cardiovascular health. It is not a medical treatment, though – think of it as part of a healthy lifestyle.

Most people with stable, well-treated blood pressure can enjoy sauna, but heat lowers blood pressure and raises the heart rate. If you have a heart condition, recent heart attack, chest pain or take blood-pressure medication, ask your doctor first, keep rounds short and avoid sudden cold plunges.

Many people continue mild sauna bathing during a normal pregnancy, but recommendations vary. Ask your doctor or midwife first, use a lower temperature, keep rounds short and leave immediately if you feel dizzy or unwell.

Children can go to the sauna with an adult, on the lower bench and at a lower temperature, for only a few minutes at a time. Always supervise them, give them water to drink and never leave a child alone in the sauna.

If you feel dizzy, sick or get a headache, leave the sauna at once, sit or lie down somewhere cool, drink water and rest. Do not go back in that day. Get medical help if the symptoms are severe or do not pass.

You can add a few drops of a sauna aroma made for sauna use to the löyly water – birch, tar, eucalyptus and pine are classics. Never pour pure essential oil on the stones; it can ignite or irritate your airways. Always dilute it in water first.

Keep towels, clothes and wood away from the heater. Check the safety distances given by the stove manufacturer, sweep the chimney regularly and install a smoke detector in the dressing room. Never dry clothes above the stove.

If an electric heater stops heating, check the fuse and the timer first. Old, crumbling stones can overheat the elements, so re-stack the stones regularly. Any electrical repairs must be done by a qualified electrician.

In Estonia the sauna has long been a place to wash, rest, heal and even give birth. Families heat the sauna on Saturdays and especially on Midsummer's Eve (jaanipäev). Common Estonian words: saun (sauna), leil (steam), viht (whisk) and kerise (stove).

Finland has millions of saunas for about 5.6 million people. Finnish sauna culture is listed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. For Finns the sauna is a place of peace – an old saying holds that in the sauna you should behave as you would in church.

keywords: after the sauna;after sauna;afterwards;dress;get dressed;evening;sleep after;after my sauna
answer: After your last round, rest until you stop sweating before you dress. Drink water and enjoy a light snack – salty food helps restore lost minerals. Many people find they sleep especially well after an evening sauna.

For a home sauna, plan for at least 1 m² of bench space per bather. Use proper insulation and a vapour barrier (foil) behind the panelling, a low door with no lock, a heater sized for the room and a working ventilation system. Use a professional for electrical work and chimney installation.

Saunamaa sells handmade birch whisks, sauna hats made from wool felt, linen towels, aspen ladles and buckets, and natural sauna aromas. Leili can explain how to use them – for orders please contact the Saunamaa shop directly.
A wool felt sauna hat protects your head from the hottest air under the ceiling, so you can stay comfortably on the upper bench. Dip it in cold water before a round for extra cooling.

Saunas have been used in Northern Europe for well over a thousand years. The earliest ones were pits dug into a hillside with heated stones; later came log-built smoke saunas. “Sauna” is a Finnish word, and it is one of the few Finnish words used all over the world.

keywords: types of sauna;kinds of sauna;different saunas;kinds;variety;which sauna is best
answer: The main types are: the traditional Finnish/Estonian sauna (hot, fairly dry air with bursts of löyly), the smoke sauna (no chimney, soft heat), the infrared sauna (warms the body directly at lower air temperature), the steam room or hammam (lower temperature but almost 100% humidity) and the Russian banya (humid, hot, with a venik whisk). Each feels different – try a few and see what you like.

keywords: infrared;ir sauna;infra red;infrared vs traditional;far infrared;cabin
answer: An infrared sauna heats your body directly with infrared panels while the air stays at about 45–60 °C. It feels gentler, heats up fast and uses little electricity, but there are no hot stones and no löyly. Fans of the traditional sauna miss the steam; people who find 80 °C too much often like infrared.

A Russian banya is usually more humid than a Finnish sauna. The steam room (parilka) is heated with a large stone stove, and bathers are patted with a venik – a whisk of birch or oak leaves – often by a banya master. Cold plunges and tea between rounds are part of the ritual.

A steam room or Turkish hammam runs at only about 40–50 °C, but the air is close to 100% humidity, so it still feels very hot. You sweat in a different way than in a dry sauna. The same rules apply: drink water, keep sessions short and cool down between rounds.

A traditional sauna has fairly dry air – roughly 10–20% relative humidity between throws. Each ladle of water on the stones raises the humidity for a moment, and that is what makes the löyly feel hotter. If the air feels harsh and dry, throw small amounts of water more often; if it feels heavy, ventilate.

topic: How often to go to the sauna
keywords: how often;every day;daily;each day;frequency;times a week;too much sauna
answer: Many Finns and Estonians go once or twice a week, and regular bathers often go almost daily. For a healthy adult, frequent sauna bathing is fine if you drink enough, keep rounds sensible and listen to your body. If you have a health condition, ask your doctor what is right for you.

keywords: best time;when to go;morning;evening;night;before bed;time of day
answer: Any time works, but many people love an evening sauna because it relaxes the body and helps sleep. A morning sauna with a cold shower can feel energising. Avoid going straight after a big meal and give yourself time to cool down afterwards.

Don’t go to the sauna on a full stomach – wait 1–2 hours after a large meal. Going very hungry isn’t great either, because you may feel faint. A light snack before and a light meal afterwards works best; salty snacks help replace the salt lost in sweat.

A sauna after exercise is a classic way to relax your muscles. Wait until your breathing and heart rate are back to normal, drink water first and start with a shorter, cooler round – your body is already warm and has lost fluid during training.

The weight you lose in the sauna is mostly water from sweating, and it comes back as soon as you drink. The sauna is not a weight-loss method – but it is a nice way to relax and recover as part of an active lifestyle.

Sweat is mostly water and salt. Your liver and kidneys do the real “detox” work. Sweating does clean your skin and pores, and many people simply feel fresh and relaxed afterwards – that is reason enough to enjoy it.

keywords: skin;pores;acne;eczema;dry skin;moisturise;moisturize;lotion;face;my skin;for my skin;good for skin
answer: Warmth and sweating open the pores and many people get a healthy glow. Wash your face before the sauna, rinse afterwards and use a moisturiser if your skin gets dry. Skin conditions such as eczema react differently from person to person – if your skin gets irritated, keep rounds short or ask a dermatologist.
Hot, dry air can dry out your hair. A wool or felt sauna hat protects both hair and head, and you can tie long hair up. Rinse your hair after the sauna and use conditioner if it feels dry.

topic: What to bring to the sauna
keywords: bring;pack;need;what do i need;checklist;flip flops;slippers;what to take;what should i bring;what to bring;bring with;bring to
answer: A simple sauna kit: a large towel to sit on, a second towel for drying, slippers or flip-flops, a water bottle, shampoo and soap, and a sauna hat if you have one. In a public sauna also bring a padlock for the locker and a swimsuit if the sauna is mixed.

Take off metal jewellery and watches – metal heats up quickly and can burn your skin. Glasses fog up and the frames can get hot, so leave them outside. Contact lenses can dry out; many people take them out or keep their eyes closed during löyly.
Leave your phone outside. Sauna heat can damage the battery and the screen, and steam gets into the electronics. Enjoy the break from screens – that is part of the point!

keywords: between rounds;break;cool down time;pause;relax between;in between
answer: Between rounds: cool down (shower, lake or fresh air), then sit or lie down for 10–15 minutes, drink water and let your heart rate settle. When you feel calm and slightly cold again, you are ready for the next round.

Shower before you enter – it is basic sauna hygiene and helps you sweat evenly. Rinse off the sweat after every round and take a proper wash with soap at the end. A cool shower is also the easiest way to cool down.

keywords: winter swimming;ice swimming;ice hole;cold water;winter;freezing;cold dip;ice bath
answer: A dip in an ice hole after the sauna is a Nordic favourite. Enter slowly, keep the dip short (from a few seconds up to about a minute), keep your head above water and never swim alone. Warm up in the sauna afterwards. People with heart or blood-pressure problems should ask a doctor before trying it.

In summer the sauna is perfect with a swim in the lake or sea between rounds. On very hot days keep the sauna a bit cooler, drink more water and rest in the shade. Midsummer’s Eve (jaanipäev) is the most popular sauna evening of the year in Estonia.

keywords: ill;sick;have a cold;common cold;caught a cold;flu;fever;infection;covid;sore throat;runny nose;colds;for a cold;with a cold;for colds
answer: Don’t go to the sauna if you have a fever, the flu or feel generally unwell – your body needs rest, and the heat adds extra strain. With a mild runny nose some people like a gentle, short sauna, but when in doubt, skip it and wait until you feel better.

Many older people enjoy the sauna for their whole life. Sit on the lower bench, use a lower temperature, keep rounds short, cool down gently (no sudden ice plunges) and drink enough water. Anyone with heart, blood-pressure or balance problems should ask their doctor first.

Some people with asthma find warm, moist air pleasant, while others find hot air or strong aromas irritating. Avoid strong essential oils, keep the temperature moderate and keep your inhaler close. Ask your doctor if you are unsure.

Heat can affect blood sugar and how fast insulin is absorbed. If you have diabetes, check your glucose before and after, keep a snack nearby, keep rounds short and ask your doctor for personal advice.

Wait until a new tattoo or piercing has fully healed – usually a few weeks – before going to the sauna. Heat, sweat and moisture slow down healing and can increase the risk of infection. Follow your tattoo artist’s aftercare advice.

topic: Sauna after an injury or surgery
answer: Avoid the sauna right after a fresh injury with swelling or after surgery – heat can increase swelling and bleeding. Ask your doctor when it is safe to go back. For old, stiff muscles the warmth often feels good.
Skip the sauna when you have sunburn. The heat makes burnt skin hurt more and slows healing. Cool the skin, drink water and wait until it has healed.

Going to the sauna during your period is perfectly fine for most people, and warmth can ease cramps. Use your usual hygiene products, sit on a towel and drink enough water. If you feel faint or unwell, keep rounds shorter.

keywords: upper bench;lower bench;top bench;where to sit;sit higher;sit lower;lying down
answer: Hot air rises, so the upper bench is the hottest place and the lower bench can be 10–20 °C cooler. Beginners, children and older people should start low. Lying down on the bench spreads the heat evenly over your body; sit up for a minute before standing to avoid dizziness.

keywords: too hot;burns;burning;ears burn;harsh;sting;stinging;nose burns;ears;my ears;burns my;hurts
answer: If the steam stings your ears or nose, the sauna is too hot for you right now. Throw smaller amounts of water, move to a lower bench, wear a sauna hat and breathe through your nose slowly. Good löyly should feel like a soft wave, not a burn.

Place the thermometer on the wall near the upper bench, at roughly head height, but not right above the heater. A hygrometer next to it shows humidity. Readings near the ceiling are always higher than at bench level.

keywords: firewood;logs;burning wood;kindling;which wood to burn;birch logs;wood to burn
answer: Use dry hardwood – birch is the Nordic classic, alder and aspen also work well. The wood should be well seasoned (moisture below about 20%). Never burn painted, glued or treated wood, plastic or rubbish – they release toxic fumes and damage the stove.

keywords: light the stove;light a fire;lighting the stove;light the fire;start fire;start a fire;make fire;kindle;fire starter;how do i light;light a;lighting a
answer: Open the damper and the air intake, put two or three logs in the firebox with small kindling and birch bark on top, and light it from the top. When the fire is going, add more logs gradually – don’t overfill the firebox. Follow your stove’s manual for the right amount of wood.

A wood-burning stove can produce carbon monoxide (CO), an invisible and odourless gas. Never close the damper while there are still glowing embers, keep the chimney clean, make sure there is fresh air and install a CO detector. Headache, dizziness or nausea can be warning signs – get into fresh air immediately.

topic: Which water to use for löyly
keywords: which water;tap water;sea water;salt water;rain water;water quality
answer: Use clean fresh water – ordinary tap water or well water is fine. Avoid sea water: salt corrodes the heater and stones. Never throw alcohol or pure essential oils on the stones. A few drops of sauna aroma diluted in the water bucket are fine.

keywords: barrel;barrel sauna;outdoor sauna;garden sauna;cabin sauna;summer house
answer: A barrel sauna is a round wooden sauna that is quick to build and heats up quickly thanks to its small volume. It is popular in gardens and summer houses. Keep it on a dry, ventilated base, protect the roof and maintain the wood every few years.

A tent sauna has a small wood stove inside a heat-resistant tent – great for camping, hiking or winter fishing trips. Keep a safe distance between the stove and the tent fabric, put the stove on a stable base and never leave the fire unattended. There are even sauna boats and sauna trailers.

Small electric saunas are common in Finnish and Estonian apartments. A space of 2–4 m² with a suitable electric heater is enough. Check building rules, use a certified electrician and make sure there is good ventilation and a waterproof floor.

topic: Running cost of an electric sauna
keywords: electricity;cost;energy;kwh;power;bill;how much does it cost;consumption;how much electricity;electricity use;use electricity;uses electricity
answer: An electric heater for a home sauna is typically 4.5–9 kW. A sauna evening of 1–2 hours often uses roughly 5–10 kWh depending on the heater, insulation and how long you heat. Multiply by your electricity price to estimate the cost – a well-insulated room saves energy.
A sauna door should open outward and must never have a lock, so you can always get out quickly. Use tempered safety glass for glass doors and windows, and a wooden handle that doesn’t get hot.

Soft, warm and dim light creates the best sauna mood. Use only lamps and LED strips rated for sauna heat and moisture, and place them low – for example under the benches or behind a wooden shade – so they don’t shine in your eyes.

A musty smell usually means the sauna doesn’t dry out properly. Ventilate after every use, leave the door open, wash the benches and floor, and check for rotten or mouldy boards that need replacing. A heating session with the door open also helps dry everything out.

keywords: paraffin;wax;varnish;paint;treat;treatment;protect wood;bench oil;sauna oil;treat the wood;varnish the benches;varnish benches;oil the benches;treat benches;paint the benches
answer: Inside the hot room, most people leave the walls untreated or use a sauna-specific protective wax or paraffin oil. Never use ordinary varnish or paint on benches – it gets sticky and can release fumes. Treat benches only with products made for saunas.

topic: How many stones the heater needs
keywords: how many stones;kg;kilograms;amount of stones;stone size;stack
answer: The heater manual says how many kilograms of stones to use – small electric heaters often take around 20–40 kg, wood stoves usually more. Stack them loosely so air can flow, with bigger stones at the bottom, and make sure the heating elements are fully covered.

Aufguss is a sauna ceremony popular in Germany and Central Europe. A sauna master pours water with aromas on the stones and wafts the hot steam to the guests with a towel, often to music. It is intense – sit lower if you are new to it.

topic: Sauna words in Estonian and Finnish
answer: Some useful sauna words (Estonian / Finnish): saun / sauna – sauna; leil / löyly – steam; viht / vihta (or vasta) – birch whisk; keris / kiuas – sauna stove; lava / lauteet – bench; kulp / kauha – ladle; saunamüts / saunahattu – sauna hat.

topic: How to use a birch whisk
keywords: use whisk;use a whisk;how to whisk;whisking;patting;technique;use a birch whisk;use the whisk;whisk correctly;correctly
answer: Soak the whisk in warm water for a few minutes. In the hot room, warm it over the stones for a moment, then gently pat your skin from feet upwards – legs, back, arms. Short, light movements are enough; a whisk should massage, not hurt. Rinse it and let it dry after use.

topic: How long a birch whisk lasts
keywords: whisk last;how long does a whisk;reuse;reuse whisk;how many times
answer: A fresh birch whisk can usually be used a few times if you rinse it and let it dry or keep it cool between sessions. Once most leaves have fallen off, it is time for a new one – old whisks make great compost.
Linen towels are light, absorbent and dry quickly. Wash them at 40–60 °C without fabric softener (it reduces absorbency) and dry them on a line. They become softer with every wash.

topic: Caring for a wooden ladle and bucket
answer: Wooden ladles and buckets should be emptied and dried after every sauna – don’t leave them standing in water. If a wooden bucket starts to leak after a long dry period, fill it with water and the wood will usually swell and seal again.

topic: Caring for a wool sauna hat
answer: Wash a wool felt sauna hat by hand in lukewarm water with a mild wool detergent, gently squeeze out the water and let it dry in its shape. Don’t put it in a tumble dryer – felt can shrink and lose its shape.

Popular sauna gifts: a wool felt sauna hat, a linen towel, a set of birch whisks, an aspen ladle and bucket, or a set of natural sauna aromas. For a beginner, a ‘first sauna kit’ with a hat, towel and aroma is a lovely idea.

For many people the sauna is a calm place away from screens and noise. The warmth, the quiet and the cool-down afterwards help them relax and unwind. It is not a treatment for mental health conditions, but it can be a pleasant part of a healthy routine.

keywords: public;spa;gym sauna;hotel sauna;swimming pool;rules in public
answer: In a public sauna: shower first, sit on a towel, follow the local swimsuit or nudity rules, ask before throwing löyly, keep conversations quiet and don’t stay too long if others are waiting. Many spas also have ‘quiet saunas’ where talking is not allowed.

keywords: voro;võro;smoke sauna estonia;estonian tradition;saaremaa;village sauna;sauna culture estonia
answer: Estonia has a rich sauna culture: the Võro smoke sauna tradition in South Estonia is listed by UNESCO, and many homes, summer houses and even offices have a sauna. Heating the sauna on Saturday and on Midsummer’s Eve, using a birch whisk and swimming in a lake or the sea are part of the tradition.

keywords: asleep;fall asleep;falling asleep;sleep in the sauna;sleepy;tired;doze
answer: Never sleep in a hot sauna – your body keeps heating up and you can overheat or faint without noticing. If you feel sleepy, it is time to get out, cool down and drink water. Don’t go to the sauna alone when you are very tired, and never after drinking alcohol.
